review.material: The complete free-access publisher text, including equations (1)–(3), was read.
review.limitations: The historical cases are recollections; earlier proofs were not rechecked.

sections.title: What it is about
sections.text: Stiny reflects on shape grammars’ history in Environment and Planning B and reconsiders the relationship between generating designs and seeing their parts.

sections.title: Central point
sections.text: Addition rules make compositions; identity rules recognize parts without changing geometry. Stiny now gives analysis and seeing greater prominence than in his early work.

sections.title: How the reflection proceeds
sections.text: He revisits his two 1976 exercises, connects addition and identity schemas through a summation schema, and describes an embedding-and-fusion cycle.

sections.title: Illustrative evidence
sections.text: The argument draws on earlier grammatical studies, contributors and personal recollections. It is not an experiment or a new comparative software evaluation.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: Structures and units can be interpreted retrospectively through rule applications, leaving room for another way of seeing at the next step.

sections.title: Reading qualification
sections.text: This brief retrospective is not a replacement for the earlier mathematical papers. Its aesthetic and historical judgments are the author’s position.

sections.title: Why read it
sections.text: Keep recognizing, changing and later describing a shape distinct. An unchanged drawing may still support new perceptual decisions.
